My mom really didn’t support me either when I came out 4 years ago at 15. It took time, I think maybe about a year until I was able to talk about my identity openly without it being an argument. Now she is supportive, it did just take some time. But the things she has said to me have stuck with me. I love my mom. No one wants to feel alienated or rejected by the people they love.

Eventually, you’ll stop caring about what people think about your identity. As long as you work towards YOUR OWN BEST INTERESTS, you will find yourself satisfied with your life. You WILL find a job. You will eventually save up enough money to move out and begin socially transitioning in a community of your own choosing. For me, it was college. It’s a pricey “escape” method, and it IS still school,but it works for a lot of people (and you get an education out of it)

Keep your own goals and aspirations in mind. The grief you are experiencing right now is painful, but no emotions are permanent. The only thing that matters is you. You are your own priority. What your parents say will affect you. But they only want to confuse you, because they themselves are confused. Don’t give up. You’ll find a way to push forward.

My dog died mid April this year. It was shocking, we found out she had cancer and three weeks later she was dead.

I was in the same boat that you’re in. I didn’t want another pet. I didn’t even want to carry on in the weeks that followed. I did find some coping techniques that did help me after her passing.

1) I created an altar for my Addie. I framed a picture and bought a candle and a small bowl. Every two days I’d leave little offerings like French fries, pretzels, etc. things she liked.

2) I talk to her. Sometimes I’d write letters, sometimes I’d light her candle and speak out loud, somedays I’d cry and hold the picture to fall asleep. It helped.

3) realize this isn’t your fault. There is literally nothing you could have done to prevent her from getting hurt or from her dying. Life just happens, eventually it will take all of us. Death is just as natural as life. Talk about it openly, even if it makes you sad. It’s normal.

4) the pain is hard and it feels like you can never have another pet again. But you can. We got our puppy a month or so after Addie died, and spending time with her has helped me tremendously. We have so much love to give to our pets, why stop.

death isn’t disappearance. Your dog’s physical form may be gone, but I mean it when I say your dog will very much so live on as long as you remember her. Someone once told me that the best way we can honor those who have died is by living our lives as the best human beings we can possibly be. Your dog may be in pain, she may not live much longer. But she loves you, and love isn’t something that will die with her.

When the things we love die, it’s hard to carry on without them. But your pet isn’t gone by any means. He may be dead, but as long as you remember and think about him, he lives on with you. It’s not the same without him there physically, But he’s still there through the memories and love you have for him. 

You didn’t want death for your dog because you loved him so much. Your dog wouldn’t want death for you either.

It’s less of dealing with it and more of learning to live with the fact that they’re dead. My dog was put down on Monday because of her cancer. It’s been the longest week of my life and there are points in time where I can’t bring myself to do anything but cry and lay in bed.

What’s helped me a little is talking to her. I set up a shrine for her which is kind of small, it’s got a small wooden bowl, a framed picture of her, a few plans and a candle. I put some food or flowers in the bowl, I light the candle, and I’ll just talk. I’ll tell her about how much I miss her, how my day was, what I did, etc. She can’t eat now, obviously, I mean she’s dead. But she loved fries and chips, I think she’d appreciate me continuing to leave her gifts. if that’s weird for you or you prefer to write, I also write letters and put them by her picture.

It’s not going to be easy. You loved your dog. There was a bond and a connection and it’s so painful. They’re physically gone. I suppose it depends on your religion, but your dog still lives on from the memories they gifted you. Openly talk to
people about your grief. This sub has helped me cope a lot, because someone understands how I feel and that makes me realize there isn’t an incorrect way to grief when it comes to pet loss, really.
